newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: China not a threat to neighbours - envoy.
newsitem.headline: China not a threat to neighbours - envoy.

text.p: Political turmoil or economic crisis in China could affect Asia's stability but the country's rise as a superpower should not worry its neighbours, a Chinese diplomat told an international security meeting on Tuesday.
Ambassador Yang Chengxu, president of the China Institute of International Relations, said China's rapid economic growth and political stability contributed to regional peace.
"If China falls into any political turmoil or serious economic difficulty, it will inevitably yield negative influence to the stability of this region," said Yang, who is based in Beijing.

Speaking at the end of a two-day seminar on Southeast Asian security and the role of external powers, Yang tried to allay fears expressed by some speakers that an emergent China would be a destabilising factor.

"The aim of certain major powers in creating the fallacy of China's threat is to deliberately drive a wedge between China and the medium- and small-sized nations in this region. The latter are also showing a little bit of concern about what will happen after China's rise."
But this is a "fallacy" and some people are overestimating China's strength, he added.

Philippine President Fidel Ramos, who addressed the meeting on Monday, said uncertainties over China's intentions in the disputed and potentially oil-rich isles in the South China Sea worried small Asian nations.
Ramos's national security adviser, Jose Almonte, told the meeting Southeast Asian nations recognised China's right to defence capabilities suitable to its status as an emerging great power.
"It is the object of China's military modernisation that ASEAN (the Association of Southeast Asian Nations) is uneasy about," he said.
Almonte added: "Taken together with rising Chinese nationalism, it becomes easy for outsiders to see China as gathering strength to 'right the wrongs of history'."
But Almonte said war was no longer a reasonable option for great powers.

He said the post-Cold War balance of power in Asia was still evolving, and predicted its probable outcome would be a five-power balance among the United States, Russia, Japan, China and a greater ASEAN, to include Burma, Laos and Cambodia.
ASEAN currently groups Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Singapore, Brunei, Vietnam and the Philippines.
Abdul Razak Baginda, director of the Malaysian Strategic Research Centre, said: "The enormous potential of this 'middle kingdom' is endless and states see this with awe...
"The future security scenario hinges on the way we manage our relations with China."
